About this citation

Written in 1888 and published in 1889; the archive cites the section and the maxim number, which is stable across editions.

### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“From the military school of life. — What does not kill me makes me stronger.”

German

“Aus der Kriegsschule des Lebens. — Was mich nicht umbringt, macht mich stärker.”

The German has two parts. The first, “From the military school of life,” is a heading Nietzsche gives the aphorism; the second is the sentence everyone quotes.

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “What does not kill me makes me stronger.”
-   “That which does not kill us makes us stronger.”

### Attribution notes

The plural “us” is the most common alteration of the German, which is first-person singular (“mich”). It sits in Twilight of the Idols among the thirty-eight “Maxims and Arrows,” which is to say in a work of compressed polemic rather than a statement of doctrine, and Nietzsche does not gloss it anywhere.

#### About Friedrich Nietzsche

Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a German classical philologist who became a radical critic of morality, metaphysics, and modern culture. Appointed professor at Basel at twenty-four, he resigned from ill health and wrote in solitude across Switzerland, Italy, and Germany.

### Interpretation

Nietzsche's remark is usually read as encouragement, which sits oddly with the rest of his work. The claim that fits his texts is narrower: resistance is what makes strength perceptible and developable, so an obstacle-free existence would leave capacities unrealised. He is not praising suffering and does not hold that hardship is beneficial in general — much of his writing is about damage that does not produce anything. The remark describes a condition of growth, not a recommendation to seek pain.

#### Why it matters

The accurate version is about response rather than event: what matters is what the difficulty calls out, which is why identical hardships produce opposite results.

#### Is the wording of this Friedrich Nietzsche quotation commonly changed?
